messages.author: 9065d041a7201790
messages.subject: Optimize bootstrapping in parallel
parts:
Dear lavaan users.

I'm trying to run some extensive simulations that require bootstrapping a lavaan model. I'm currently using the boot package with either snow or multicore parallel computing on a strong Linux machine (24 cores...). However it still takes too much time (two weeks for the whole thing...). I was wondering if anyone has any experience and suggestions of how to optimize the bootstrap to speed things up.

Thanks!
Isaac.

messages.author: bfa43814f6ba1969
messages.subject: Re: Optimize bootstrapping in parallel
parts:
Hi,

Three suggestions:

1) If you are running a Monte Carlo simulation that does bootstrap in each Monte Carlo replication, then it is easier to parallelize on the Monte Carlo level than the bootstrap level

2) Throwing more hardware to the problem is an easy way to significantly speed up things. If your university has a computer cluster, you might be able to run the simulation with 2400 instead of 24 cores. 

3) Instead of using boot on one of the main lavaan functions (sem, cfa), prepare the starting values and parse the model before bootstrapping and then apply bootstrap to private functions that do the actual estimation. You can use profiling http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Profiling.html to see where the code spends time and if you can move some of that to preprocessing.

4) decrease the number of iterations to exit problematic estimations more quickly.

What exactly is the best way depends on what specifically you want to do with bootstrap. 

Mikko

parts: Hi,

On 29 Nov 2017, at 19:40 , Itzik Fradkin <idif...@gmail.com> wrote:

Dear Mikko.

Thanks for the suggestions. A few questions:

1. Why would that be faster? I think I tried that and it seemed slower.... Maybe I did it wrong?
It may not be faster, but is easier to implement. If it was substantially slower, then you did something incorrectly.
3. Can you explain a bit more how is it done? If you have an example code for it that would be great.

The link provides you instructions for profiling and there you can identify the optimization function. In theory, you could call nlminb directly to avoid some overhead, but that the performance gains may not be that large.

This approach will require a bit technical competence and R programming.
4. I can decrease the number of iteration. It's 1000 right now. I'm afraid any less than that going to be not enough for stable CIs. What do you mean by 'exit problematic estimations more quickly’?

I mean the number of iteration that the optimizer is allowed to try before declaring non-convergence, not the number of bootstrap replications.

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/lavaan/3zCqlADa0k0/Sci0__2jiS8J

Mikko

Thanks!!!
